overview.body:
**Agni** ​(*agni*) — ‌Fire, the ‌Sacrifice, the ​Messenger · ​the god ​of fire, ​the fire ​of ‌the stomach, ​digestive faculty, ​gastric fluid ‌— belongs ​to the ‌Sanskrit tradition, ​where it ‌is ​catalogued under ​the domain ​"Fire, Sacrifice, ​Messenger". The ​name means ‌"the god ​of fire, ‌the ​fire of ‌the stomach, ​digestive faculty, ‌gastric fluid"[^1].

​**Agni** is ‌fire worshipped ​as a ​god: ‌the flame ‌that carries ‌every offering ​upward, the ​guest in ‌every home’s ​hearth, the ​priest ‌of the ​gods and ​the god ‌of priests. ​Second only ‌to Indra ​in Vedic ​hymns, ​he is ​the most ‌frequently invoked ‌deity at ​the ritual ‌itself — ​for without ​Agni, ‌no prayer ‌reaches heaven.[^2]

‌PuniCodex restores ‌the name ​as **Agni** ‌and serves ​its temple ​at ​[its temple](https://punicodex.com/agni/). ‌The restoration ​aSCII-equivalent form ​— a ​description computed ‌from the ​displayed form ​itself. ​The plain ‌ASCII form ​*agni* survives ‌as a ​modern convenience ‌imposed by ​the early ‌domain-name ‌system; the ​restoration, not ​the fallback, ​is the ​form the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

the-name.body:
The ​name ‌is ‌attested in ​Devanagari ​as ​**अग्नि**. ​Etymologically ​it ‌means "the ​god ​of ‌fire, ​the ‌fire ​of the ‌stomach, ​digestive ​faculty, ​gastric ​fluid"[^1].

​The ASCII ‌form ​*agni* ‌survives ​only ‌because the ​early ‌domain-name ​system ‌could ​not ​carry diacritics; ‌it ‌is ‌a ​technological ​compromise, ‌not an ​ancient ​spelling. ‌The ​Unicode ​restoration ‌**Agni** recovers ​the ‌full ​diacritic ​detail ​of ​the scholarly ‌transliteration ‌directly ​in ‌the ​address ​bar. The ‌restoration ‌aSCII-equivalent ‌form ‌— ​a ‌description computed ​from ​the ​displayed ‌form ​itself.

The ​letter-by-letter ​transformation ‌runs:

- ​**a** ​→ ​**A** — ‌Same
- ​**g** ‌→ ​**g** ‌— ​Same
- **n** ‌→ ‌**n** ​— ​Same
- ​**i** ​→ **i** ‌— ‌Short ​/i/

pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation ‌of ​the name ​is ​**/ˈɑːɡni/** ​— ​Sanskrit ‌(IAST: ​Agni).[^1]

​Phoneme ‌by phoneme:

- ​**Ag-** ‌— ​The ‌a ​is ​the ​open ​“ah”; g ​is ‌a ​hard ‌stop. ​The ‌name ​IS ‌the common ​noun ‌“fire”.
- ​**-ni** ​— ‌Palatal ‌n ‌with ​a long ​ī ‌in ​Vedic ​lengthening; ‌the ​word ​carries ‌its own ​glow.

‌For ​the ​modern ​speaker, ​the ‌closest ‌approximation is: ​“AHG-nee”

‌Kindred ​and ​historical ‌forms ‌of ‌the ‌name:

- **Avestan** ​— ‌Atar
- ​**Latin** ​— ​ignis
- ‌**English** ​— ​“ignite” — ​the ‌Indo-European ​fire-word ​family

​His ‌name ​is ‌cognate with ​Latin ‌ignis: ​the ‌god ‌and ​the ​element ​share one ​root ‌across ‌three ​millennia.

domains.body:
**Agni** ​is fire ‌worshipped ‌as a ​god: the ​flame ​that carries ​every ​offering upward, ‌the guest ​in ​every home’s ‌hearth, ​the priest ‌of ​the gods ‌and the ​god ​of priests. ​Second ​only to ​Indra ‌in Vedic ​hymns, he ‌is ​the most ‌frequently ​invoked deity ‌at the ​ritual ‌itself — ​for ​without Agni, ‌no ‌prayer reaches ‌heaven.[^1]

### The ​Messenger

​Every offering ‌is ​carried to ​the ‌gods through ​his flame ​— ‌Agni is ​the ‌one channel ​of prayer.

### ​Threefold ​Fire

He ​has ‌three births ‌— ​in the ‌heavens as ​sun, ​in the ‌waters ‌as lightning, ‌on ‌earth as ​the hearth-flame.

### ‌The ​Divine Priest

​Hotṛ ​of the ‌gods, he ​conducts ​the rite ​he ‌is offered ​at ​— god ​and officiant ‌in ​one flame.

### ‌Consumer ​and Purifier

‌He ​eats the ‌oblation and ‌burns ​away sin; ​the ​dead pass ​through his ‌mouth ‌to the ​fathers.

symbols.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated with ‌Agni ​concentrates ​in ​a ​small set ​of ‌recurring ​attributes, ​each ‌a compressed ​statement ‌about ​the ‌name:[^1]

- **The ​Messenger** ​— ​Every ​offering ​is carried ‌to ​the ‌gods ​through his ‌flame ​— ‌Agni ​is ‌the one ​channel ​of ‌prayer.
- ‌**Threefold ‌Fire** — ​He ​has ‌three ​births — ​in ‌the ​heavens ​as ‌sun, in ​the ‌waters ​as ​lightning, ​on earth ​as ‌the ‌hearth-flame.
- ​**The Divine ‌Priest** ​— ​Hotṛ ‌of ‌the gods, ‌he ‌conducts ​the ‌rite ​he is ​offered ​at ‌— ​god and ​officiant ​in ‌one ​flame.
- ​**Consumer and ​Purifier** ‌— ​He ‌eats the ​oblation ‌and ​burns ‌away ‌sin; the ​dead ​pass ​through ​his ‌mouth to ‌the ​fathers.

mythology.body:
Agni’s mythology ​is less narrative than ‌elemental: he is ‌born daily from the ​friction-sticks, devours his ​parents (the sticks that ​bore him) at ​birth, and carries the ​sacrifice skyward. Yet ‌the Vedic poets gave ​him a full ​biography — hidden at ‌birth, stolen by ​the gods, established among ‌men — and ​the epics gave him ‌a genealogy and ​a role in every ​hero’s fire-drill.[^1]

### The ​Hidden Birth (Rigveda 10.129)

​The birth-hymns tell ​that Agni was concealed ‌in the waters ​and the wood, ‌secret like a son ​hidden by his ‌mother, until the ten ​sisters — the ‌fingers of the kindling-priest ​— rubbed him ‌forth. ‘The new-born infant ​licks the earth’: ​the first flame tasting ‌the world it ‌will consume and consecrate.[^2]

### ‌Agni Flees the ​Sacrifice (Rigveda 10.51)

In ​the great dialogue ‌hymn, Agni hides from ​the burden of ​the office — the ‌god who must ​eat the offering shrinks ​from being eaten ‌by his own hunger. ​The gods find ‌him in the waters, ​the fig-tree, the ​plants; each offers to ​hide him; he ​returns to the ritual ‌because prayer without ‌fire goes nowhere. It ​is the most ‌psychologically modern of Vedic ​hymns.

### The Stolen ​Fire of the Gods ‌(Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa)

The ‌Brāhmaṇas narrate how the ‌gods kept Agni ‌from men until Mātariśvan, ​the Vedic Prometheus, ‌brought him down hidden ​in the stalk ​of a plant — ​the mythic warrant ‌for the fire-drill ​itself, and for the ​conviction that fire ​is heaven’s property on ‌loan to the ​hearth.

### Agni and the ​Khandava Forest (Mahābhārata)

​In the epic, Agni, ‌weakened by a ​surfeit of ghee, begs ‌Krishna and Arjuna ​to let him burn ‌the Khandava forest; ​fed by the conflagration, ‌he blazes up ‌again as of old. ​The episode fixes ​the epic’s theology of ​fire: indiscriminate when ​ravenous, a god still, ‌and the friend ‌of heroes who understand ​his hunger.

syncretism.body:
Agni ​is ‌the Vedic ‌counterpart ​of ​the ​Avestan ​Atar, and ​the ‌fire-cult ​is ​the ‌one element ​Zoroastrianism ‌kept ​most ‌fully ​from the ​old ​Indo-Iranian ​religion. ​Greek ‌writers compared ​him ‌to ​Hephaestus ‌and ​the altar-flame; ‌modern ​linguistics ‌binds ​him ​to Latin ‌ignis ‌and ‌English ​ignite. ​In Hindu ‌ritual ​he ​remains ‌unpolluted ​by sect ​— ‌every ​saṃskāra ‌from birth ​to ​cremation ​passes ​through ‌him.[^1]

Kindred ‌figures ​in ‌the ​PuniCodex ​cross-tradition index ‌include ‌[[brigid|Brigid]] ‌(fire ‌/ ​poetry / ‌inspiration), ​[[eshu|Ẹṣù]] ​(messenger ​/ ‌travel / ​commerce), ​[[gna|Gná]] ​(messenger ‌/ ​travel / ​commerce), ​[[hanuman|Hanumān]] ‌(messenger ​/ ‌travel / ​commerce), ‌[[hephaistos|Hēphaistos]] ​(fire ‌/ ‌forge / ​craft), ​and ​[[hermes|Hermês]] ​(messenger ‌/ travel ‌/ ​commerce).
